description.narrative:
Webbed Waters: Diplomacy as Adaptive Practice Introduction Rivers often find room for themselves, and most often they do not respect borders. This fact is well illustrated by the multiple stories of shifting rivers in the Himalayas. This course intends to explorequestions around resilient treaties. In other words, it pushes one to reflect on: why some Treaties work while others fail. To do this students are exposed to methodological tools and concepts which sit at the intersection of International Relations, Network Theory, and Environmental Studies. Traditional approaches to water diplomacy are often built around rational frameworks where there is an overwhelming focus on water allocations and demand-supply equations. These meta-narratives on water diplomacy are often distant from micro-narratives which are indicative of how treaties are lived and experienced by the people. In our quest to find an answer to this problem, we shall study water diplomacy as an adaptive practice, illustrating that diplomacy is often embedded in networks and practices. Diplomacy can also be understood as a system of relationships that shifts as rivers, climate and power dynamics change. Thus, the course makes a very conscious shift from rational diplomacy to relational diplomacy. The course will span 2.5 months (taught on weekends for 2 hrs) and will be delivered online. There will be three in-person gatherings. A workshop to launch the course, afield visit to see adaptation in action, and a conference where students present their research. Together, these will culminate in a co-authored book. The course will be led by the Department of International Relations, South Asian University. It will partner with three institutes from South Asia: Royal University of Bhutan, Bhutan, ICIMOD, Nepal and BIISS, Bangladesh. The partners will contribute in intellectual, logistical, and field capacities to this project. Outcomes • Certificate course for participating students •Research Output (co-authored volume by all contributors). We can think of policy briefs and working papers for students. • Developing a Regional Network on Adaptive Diplomacy • Foundation for ongoing research and collaboration. • Formal partnership through MoUs. Envisioned collaboration • Codesign and codelivery of the course. We can also solicit specific units to experts, if required or havesome senior scholars in advisory capacity. A draft syllabus will be circulated by SAU, which can be revised and revisited to add to individual expertise. • Mentoring students for research projects. 4 from each country. Total number of students can be 16. • Jointfacilitation of field visits and workshops. Students selection criteria
• Must be recommended and nominated by these four institutions. We can have an open call for some days. The selection committee can be of nodal persons for this project and OXFAM. • Studentsshould be in their fourth year, final master’s or early PhD scholars. • Should be familiar with International Relations, Environmental Studies, International Law, and Network Studies.
Take Aways from the Course
• Familiarise students with relational and adaptive frameworks to understand water diplomacy. • Introduce students to a methodological and conceptual toolkit for analysing transboundary water governance and diplomacy. • Expose students to empirical case studies and applied case analysis on Adaptation and Resilience in Water Diplomacy. • Facilitate Network on Water Diplomacy and Practice, with connections across four South Asian Institutions. • Offer students skills with applied research experience and professional input.

participating-org.narrative: The South Asian University (SAU)was established by an inter-ministerial Agreement among SAARC member countries in 2007 and was opened to students in 2010. The mandate of the SAU, up envisages that the choice of the programs of studies to be offered at this University should: *enhance learning in the South Asian community that promotes an understanding of each other’s perspectives and strengthen regional consciousness.· * provide liberal and humane education to the brightest and the most dedicated students of South Asia so that a new class of quality leadership is nurtured.· * enhance capacity building of the South Asian Nations in science, technology and other areas of higher learning vital for improving their quality of life such as information technology, biotechnology and management sciences, etc.· The Department of International Relations at the South Asian seeks to widen our appreciation of the content of the international by interrogating intellectual traditions within SouthAsia as embedded in the larger Asia. Thefaculty of the Department share wide-ranging research interests. These encompass both mainstream theories and critical approaches to the study of International Relations, disciplinary histories of IR, global political economy concerns and international normative political theory.
